name: Database Management Systems
desc: Schema, catalog, users, ER model, relational algebra, SQL, FDs, normalization, indexing, transactions, concurrency, recovery

topics.name: DBMS Concepts, Schema, Catalog & Users
notes: **Schema** = description/structure of the database (changes rarely, defined at design time). **Database state (instance/snapshot)** = the data stored at a particular moment.
**Catalog / data dictionary** stores **metadata** (data about data: table definitions, types, constraints, users). Self-describing nature of a DBMS.
**Three-schema architecture**: internal (physical) level, conceptual (logical) level, external (view) level. A user sees an **external view** (e.g. a net-banking screen).

**Logical data independence**: change the conceptual schema without changing external schemas/apps. **Physical data independence**: change the internal schema (storage, indexes) without changing the conceptual schema. Logical is **harder** to achieve.
**Pre-compiler** extracts embedded DML (SQL) statements from a host-language program (e.g. C) and sends them to the DML compiler.

**DBMS users**: **Naive (parametric) end users** use canned transactions/forms (bank clerk, ATM users). **Casual users** occasionally query using a query language. **Sophisticated users** (engineers, analysts) write complex queries using tools. **Standalone users** use ready-made packages. Plus the **DBA**, database designers and application programmers.
**Architectures**: single-tier (standalone, everything on one machine), two-tier (client ↔ DB server), three-tier (client ↔ application server ↔ DB server — web apps).
Database types: **textual/document databases** (research documents), multimedia, GIS, data warehouses (analytics).

b: A **Database Management System** stores data in an organised way and lets many users read and update it safely (MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL).
💡 A library catalogue instead of a pile of books.
- **Schema** = the design/structure (changes rarely).
- **State / instance** = the actual data right now (a snapshot at 4 pm).
- **Catalog / data dictionary** = stores **metadata** ("data about data").
Internal (storage) → Conceptual (tables) → External (what each user sees — a **view**).
- **Physical independence**: change storage without touching the tables.
- **Logical independence**: change tables without breaking apps (harder).
- **Naive users**: use ready-made screens (ATM, bank clerk).
- **Casual users**: occasional queries.
- **Sophisticated users**: experts writing complex queries.
The **pre-compiler** pulls SQL out of C/Java programs. Architectures: 1-tier (standalone), 2-tier, 3-tier (web apps).

topics.name: Entity–Relationship Model
notes: **Entity** (rectangle), **attribute** (oval), **relationship** (diamond). "Student registers Course" → "registers" goes **inside a diamond** between the two rectangles.

Attribute types: **Simple/atomic**, **Composite** (address → door no, street, city, zip; phone → country code + number), **Multivalued** (double oval — phone numbers), **Derived** (dashed oval — age from DOB, experience from date of joining), **Key** (underlined).

**Weak entity** (double rectangle): has no key of its own, depends on an **identifying owner** through an **identifying relationship** (double diamond), with **total participation** and **existence dependency**. Identified by a partial key + the owner's key.
**Cardinality ratios**: 1:1, 1:N, M:N. "Student registers for many courses" (and courses have many students) → **M:N**.
**Participation**: total (double line, every entity must participate) or partial.
**Role** = the function an entity plays in a relationship (Instructor "teaches"). **Recursive relationship**: the same entity set appears twice (Employee supervises Employee).

**Specialization** (top-down): divide an entity into subclasses (MovieZone → Hollywood, Bollywood). **Generalization** (bottom-up): combine common entities into a superclass (SENSE, SELECT, SCOPE → DEPARTMENTS). Subclasses **inherit** all superclass attributes.
A **relationship set** is the verb ("Customer **buys** Products" → Buys). Attributes like ProductName are not entity sets.

slides.t: 🧩 The ER model — drawing the database
b: - **Entity** (rectangle): a thing — Student, Course
- **Attribute** (oval): a property — name, age
- **Relationship** (diamond): an action linking entities — "registers"
- **Composite**: has parts (address → street, city, zip)
- **Multivalued** (double oval): many values (phone numbers)
- **Derived** (dashed oval): calculated (age from date of birth)
- **Key** (underlined): unique (ProjectId)
- 1:1, 1:N, **M:N** (students ↔ courses)
- **Weak entity** (double rectangle): can't be identified on its own; depends on an **owner** through an identifying relationship (total participation + existence dependency).
- **Specialization** (top-down): MovieZone → Hollywood, Bollywood
- **Generalization** (bottom-up): SENSE, SELECT, SCOPE → DEPARTMENTS
Subclasses **inherit all** attributes of the superclass.

topics.name: Relational Model, Keys & Constraints
notes: **Relation** = table; **tuple** = row; **attribute** = column; **domain** = set of allowed values; **degree** = number of attributes; **cardinality** = number of tuples.

**Super key**: any set of attributes that uniquely identifies tuples. **Candidate key**: minimal super key. **Primary key**: the chosen candidate key. **Alternate keys**: the other candidate keys. **Foreign key**: refers to the primary key of another relation.
Number of super keys of R with n attributes and a single-attribute key: **2^(n−1)**. With 8 attributes → 2⁷ = 128.
**Constraints**: **Domain**, **Key** (uniqueness), **Entity integrity** (primary key can't be NULL), **Referential integrity** (a foreign key must match an existing primary key or be NULL).
**Prime attribute** = part of some candidate key. **Non-prime** = not part of any candidate key.

b: Relation = **table**, tuple = **row**, attribute = **column**.
**Degree** = number of columns; **cardinality** = number of rows.
- **Super key**: any set of columns that identifies a row
- **Candidate key**: a **minimal** super key
- **Primary key**: the chosen candidate key
- **Foreign key**: points to another table's primary key
With n attributes and a 1-attribute key → **2ⁿ⁻¹** super keys (8 attributes → 128).
- **Entity integrity**: primary key can't be NULL
- **Referential integrity**: a foreign key must match an existing key (or be NULL)

topics.name: Relational Algebra
notes: **σ (select/sigma)** picks **rows** satisfying a condition: σ country='India' (store). **π (project/pi)** picks **columns**: π city (store) ≈ SELECT city FROM store (but π removes duplicates).
**∪, −, ∩** need **union-compatible** relations (same degree and domains). **×** Cartesian product: degree adds, cardinality multiplies.
**⋈ natural join** = × + equality on common attributes + remove the duplicate columns. **θ-join** uses any condition. Outer joins keep unmatched tuples.
**÷ division** answers "for all" queries (students who took ALL courses).
**ρ (rename)**. Fundamental operations: σ, π, ∪, −, ×, ρ (∩ and ⋈ can be derived).

b: The maths behind SQL.
- **σ (select)** picks **rows**: σ country='India'(store)
- **π (project)** picks **columns**: π city(store) = SELECT city FROM store
- **∪, −, ∩**: need tables with the same columns
- **× (Cartesian product)**: columns add, rows multiply
- **⋈ (join)**: match rows on common columns
- **÷ (division)**: "for ALL" questions (students who took every course)

topics.name: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Queries
notes: **DDL** (structure): CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME. **DML** (data): SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. **DCL** (permissions): GRANT, REVOKE. **TCL** (transactions): COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.
`SELECT DISTINCT col` removes duplicate values. `SELECT *` returns all columns. `UPDATE t SET col = 'new' WHERE col = 'old'` changes values.
**WHERE** filters rows before grouping; **HAVING** filters groups after **GROUP BY**. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
**DELETE** removes rows (can have WHERE, can be rolled back, DML). **TRUNCATE** removes all rows fast (DDL). **DROP** removes the whole table.
Pattern matching: `LIKE 'A%'` (% = any string, _ = one character). NULL checks use `IS NULL`, never `= NULL`.
Joins: INNER, LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER. Subqueries can be used in WHERE/HAVING (e.g. avg salary greater than the company average).

b: - **DDL** (structure): CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
- **DML** (data): SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
- **DCL** (permissions): GRANT, REVOKE
- **TCL** (transactions): COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
- `SELECT DISTINCT city FROM t` → no duplicates
- `SELECT * …` → all columns
- `UPDATE People SET LastName='Singh' WHERE LastName='Mishra'`
- `WHERE name LIKE 'A%'`; `WHERE x IS NULL`
- **WHERE** filters rows (before grouping)
- **GROUP BY** makes groups
- **HAVING** filters groups (after grouping)
Departments where the average salary of male employees beats the company average: WHERE sex='M' GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > (subquery).

topics.name: Functional Dependencies, Closure & Candidate Keys
notes: **X → Y**: equal X values imply equal Y values. **Armstrong's axioms**: reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity (+ derived: union, decomposition, pseudo-transitivity).
**Attribute closure X⁺**: start with X, repeatedly add the right side of any FD whose left side is inside the set. X is a super key if X⁺ = all attributes.
**Finding candidate keys**: attributes that never appear on any RHS **must be in every key**. Then try adding attributes until the closure covers everything; keep only minimal sets.
**Extraneous attribute**: in AB → C, A is extraneous if B⁺ already contains C.
**Lossless join** decomposition of R into R1, R2: **R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2** (the common attributes form a key of one part).
**Dependency preservation**: (F1 ∪ F2)⁺ = F⁺.

b: **X → Y**: if two rows have the same X, they must have the same Y.
Example: RollNo → Name.
Start with X, keep adding anything an FD lets you reach.
If X⁺ contains every attribute → X is a **super key**.
Example: AB → C, C → DE, E → F gives AB⁺ = ABCDEF.
Attributes that **never appear on the right side** must be in every key. Then grow the set until its closure covers everything, and keep only minimal sets.
AB→CD, D→B, C→A → keys AB, AD, BC, CD (**4**).
Splitting R into R1 and R2 is **lossless** if the common columns are a **key of one side**.

topics.name: Normalization: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF
notes: **1NF**: all values atomic (no repeating groups or multivalued cells).
**2NF**: 1NF + **no partial dependency** (no non-prime attribute depends on part of a candidate key). Any relation with single-attribute keys only is automatically 2NF.
**3NF**: 2NF + **no transitive dependency** of non-prime attributes. Test for every X → A: X is a super key **or** A is prime.
**BCNF**: for every non-trivial X → A, **X is a super key**. BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF (BCNF is stronger). **Every 2-attribute relation is in BCNF**.

Decomposition: **3NF lossless + dependency-preserving is always possible**. **BCNF lossless is always possible but may NOT preserve dependencies** ("lossless BCNF that preserves dependencies isn't always possible").
Normalisation reduces **redundancy** and **update, insert and delete anomalies**.
**4NF** removes multivalued dependencies; BCNF does not guarantee 4NF.

b: Goal: less duplicate data and fewer **update/insert/delete anomalies**.
- **1NF**: every cell holds one value (atomic)
- **2NF**: no non-key column depends on **part** of a key
- **3NF**: no non-key column depends on another non-key column (transitive)
- **BCNF**: for every FD X → A, **X is a super key**
BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF.
- Any table with **2 attributes** is in BCNF.
- **3NF**: lossless + dependency-preserving decomposition always possible.
- **BCNF**: lossless always possible, but may **lose dependencies**.
- D → B where B is part of a key → 3NF but not BCNF.

topics.name: Indexing, B-Trees, B+ Trees & Hashing
notes: **Primary index**: on the ordering key field of a sorted file. **Clustering index**: data records are ordered (or nearly) the same way as the index entries. **Secondary index**: on a non-ordering field (always dense).
**Dense index**: an entry for every search-key value. **Sparse index**: entries for only some values (one per block).
**Multilevel index**: the first level is the index on the data file; an index built on the first level is the **second level**, and so on.
**B-tree of order m**: max m children, **max m − 1 keys**; non-root internal nodes have at least ⌈m/2⌉ children → **min ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys**. Order 4 → keys 1..3.

**B+ tree**: all data pointers in the **leaves**; internal nodes hold only keys for navigation; leaves are **linked** → fast **range queries**. Height-balanced (all leaves at the same depth). Height ≈ ⌈log_{⌈n/2⌉} N⌉ in the worst case (4 KB nodes, 40-byte entries, 1 million keys → 4).

**Hash index**: O(1) average for **equality** search (=), useless for range queries. **B+ tree index**: supports equality **and range**/ordered queries. A **hashed file** computes the record's position from its key.
Indexes speed up reads but slow down inserts/updates/deletes (indexes must be maintained), especially with large keys.

b: An index helps find rows fast without scanning the whole table. Faster reads, but slower inserts/updates.
- **Dense**: an entry for every value; **sparse**: only some.
- **Clustered**: data stored in the same order as the index.
Balanced trees designed for disks.
- Order m: up to **m − 1 keys**, at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 (order 4 → 1 to 3 keys).
- **B+ tree**: data pointers only in **leaves**, and leaves are **linked** → great for **range queries**. All leaves are at the same depth.
- **Hash**: super fast for **equality** (id = 5), useless for ranges.
- **B+ tree**: equality **and** ranges (BETWEEN, <, ORDER BY).

topics.name: Transactions, ACID & Serializability
notes: **ACID**: **Atomicity** (all or nothing — recovery manager), **Consistency** (valid state to valid state — programmer/constraints), **Isolation** (concurrent ≈ serial — concurrency-control manager), **Durability** (committed changes survive any failure — recovery manager).
Goals of concurrent execution: better **resource utilisation**, higher **throughput**, lower **waiting/response time**. (NOT a reduced chance of deadlock — concurrency makes deadlocks possible.)
**Conflicting operations**: different transactions, same data item, and **at least one is a write** (R-W, W-R, W-W).

**Conflict serializable** ⇔ the **precedence graph** (edge Ti → Tj for each conflict where Ti's op comes first) is **acyclic**. Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable, not vice versa (blind writes).

**Recoverable schedule**: if Tj reads from Ti, then Ti commits before Tj. Reading uncommitted data (dirty read) and committing first can make a schedule **irrecoverable**. **Cascadeless**: read only committed data. **Strict**: no read/write of an item until the last writer commits/aborts.
A schedule must keep the order of operations **within** each transaction.

b: A transaction = a group of operations treated as one unit (e.g. a bank transfer).
- **Atomicity**: all or nothing
- **Consistency**: valid → valid
- **Isolation**: transactions don't interfere
- **Durability**: once committed, it survives any crash
Two operations **conflict** if they come from different transactions, touch the same item, and at least one is a **write**.
**Conflict serializable** = the precedence graph has **no cycle**.
Reading uncommitted data (**dirty read**) is dangerous.
**Recoverable**: if T2 reads from T1, T1 must commit first. A cascadeless schedule reads only committed data.

topics.name: Concurrency Control: Locking, Timestamps & Isolation Levels
notes: **Lock-based**: shared (S, read) and exclusive (X, write) locks. **Two-phase locking (2PL)**: growing phase (acquire only) then shrinking phase (release only) → guarantees **conflict serializability** (but not deadlock freedom).
**Strict 2PL**: hold all **exclusive** locks until commit/abort → schedules are serializable **and strict (hence recoverable, cascadeless)**. **Rigorous 2PL**: hold all locks until commit.

**Timestamp ordering**: older transactions get priority; operations out of timestamp order are rejected (rollback). **Thomas' write rule**: ignore obsolete writes → allows some **view-serializable but not conflict-serializable** schedules. **Multiversion timestamp** allows everything basic TO allows, and more.
Other techniques: **validation (optimistic)**, **multiversion**, **multiple granularity** locking. Deadlock handling: wait-die, wound-wait, timeouts, wait-for graphs.
**Lock granularity**: **row-level** locking gives the highest concurrency (more overhead); table-level gives the least.

**Isolation levels** (weakest → strongest): **Read uncommitted** (dirty reads allowed), **Read committed** (no dirty reads), **Repeatable read** (no dirty or non-repeatable reads, **phantoms still possible**), **Serializable** (none).
**Two-phase COMMIT (2PC)** coordinates atomic commit across distributed sites (prepare/vote, then commit/abort). It is a commit protocol, not a recovery technique like deferred/immediate update.

b: Lets many transactions run at once while keeping results correct.
**Two-phase locking (2PL)**: growing phase (only take locks), then shrinking phase (only release) → **serializable**, but deadlocks are still possible.
**Strict 2PL**: hold write locks until commit → also recoverable.
Older transactions get priority; out-of-order operations are rolled back.
**Thomas' write rule** ignores outdated writes → allows some view-serializable schedules.
- Read uncommitted (dirty reads OK)
- Read committed (no dirty reads)
- **Repeatable read** (no dirty or non-repeatable reads, but phantoms are possible)
- Serializable (nothing)
**Row-level** locks give the most concurrency.

topics.name: Recovery Methods
notes: **Transaction failure** is handled by **rollback (undo)** using the log. System crash → redo committed and undo uncommitted transactions. Disk failure → restore a backup + the log.
**Log-based recovery**: write-ahead logging (**WAL**) — log records go to stable storage **before** the data page is written.
**Deferred update** (NO-UNDO/REDO): changes are written to the DB only after commit → only REDO is needed. **Immediate update** (UNDO/REDO): the DB may be updated before commit → both UNDO and REDO.
**Checkpoints** limit how much of the log must be scanned after a crash.
**Shadow paging**: keep a shadow page table; on commit switch to the new one — no log needed for undo.
**ARIES**: industrial algorithm with analysis, redo and undo passes.
**Two-phase commit is NOT a recovery technique** (it's a distributed commit protocol).

b: - Transaction failure → **rollback (undo)**.
- Crash → **redo** committed work, **undo** unfinished work, using the **log**.
- **Write-ahead logging**: write the log before the data.
- **Deferred update**: write to the DB only after commit → redo only
- **Immediate update**: may write early → undo + redo
- **Checkpoints**: less log to scan
- **Shadow paging**: keep an old copy of the page table
❌ Two-phase **commit** is not a recovery technique.

topics.name: NoSQL & Modern Databases
notes: **NoSQL** (non-relational) databases handle huge volumes of **unstructured/semi-structured** data, scale **horizontally**, and are **schema-less** (insert data without a predefined schema).
**NoSQL types**: **Key-value** (Redis, DynamoDB), **Document** (MongoDB, CouchDB), **Wide-column / column-family** (Cassandra, HBase), **Graph** (Neo4j).
**NewSQL**: relational/SQL with NoSQL-like scalability (e.g. Google Spanner, CockroachDB) — still needs a schema.

**CAP theorem**: a distributed system can guarantee at most two of **Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance**. Many NoSQL systems favour availability (BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent).

b: Databases without fixed tables, built for huge, flexible (often **unstructured**) data and easy scaling. **No predefined schema** needed.
- **Key-value**: Redis
- **Document**: MongoDB
- **Wide-column**: Cassandra, HBase
- **Graph**: Neo4j
**CAP theorem**: you can only fully have two of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance.

A constraint, not a SELECT keyword (standard SQL).

questions.q: SELECT * FROM player WHERE num_of_matches>100 AND country=’India’; What fields will be outputted by the above SQL query?
questions.h: * = all columns. WHERE only filters rows.

questions.q: Which of the following SQL queries can be used to change “Mishra” to “Singh” in the “LastName” column in the People relation?
o: UPDATE People SET LastName=’Mishra’ INTO LastName=’Singh’
UPDATE People SET LastName=’Singh’ WHERE LastName=’Mishra’
MODIFY People SET LastName=’Mishra’ INTO LastName=’Singh’
MODIFY People SET LastName=’Singh’ WHERE LastName=’Mishra’
w: UPDATE … SET new value … WHERE old condition.
questions.h: UPDATE table SET col = new WHERE col = old.

questions.q: Consider Emp(Empcode, Name, Sex, Salary, Deptt) and the query: SELECT Deptt FROM Emp WHERE sex = 'M' GROUP BY Deptt HAVING avg(Salary) > (SELECT avg(Salary) FROM Emp). The output will be the departments where:
o: Average salary of male employees is more than the average salary of the organization
Average salary of male employees is equal to the average salary of the organization
Average salary of male employees is the average salary of the organization
Average salary of male employees is less than the average salary of the organization
w: WHERE keeps males, GROUP BY department, HAVING compares with the overall average.
questions.h: WHERE → rows, GROUP BY → groups, HAVING → filter groups.

questions.q: Which clause filters groups created by GROUP BY?
CREATE, ALTER and DROP are which type of SQL commands?
INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE belong to:
GRANT and REVOKE are:
COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT are:
Which command removes all rows of a table quickly, keeps the structure, and is a DDL command?
w: DML, row by row, can use WHERE.
questions.h: DELETE (DML) vs TRUNCATE (DDL) vs DROP (table gone).

questions.q: To find employees whose name starts with 'A', use:
w: That means the second character is A.

questions.q: The correct way to check for missing values in SQL is:
w: Comparisons with NULL are never true.

questions.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp counts:
o: All rows, including rows with NULLs
Only non-NULL values of the first column

questions.q: What is the number of candidate keys for a relation R(A,B,C,D) having functional dependencies {AB->CD, D->B, C->A}?
w: AB, AD (D→B), BC (C→A) and CD (C→A, D→B) all determine everything.
questions.h: Swap attributes using FDs: B↔D (D→B), A↔C (C→A).

questions.q: In a relation R(A,B,C,D) having functional dependencies {AB->CD, D->B}, the extraneous attribute in AB->CD is
w: C is on the right side; removing it would lose information.
Neither A nor B alone determines CD.
questions.h: Extraneous: check the closure of the remaining LHS.

questions.q: In the relation R(A,B,C,D,E,F) with functional dependencies {AB->C, C->DE, E->F, D->A, C->B}, AB+ is
w: AB → C → DE → F; closure includes A, B.
questions.h: Closure always includes the starting attributes.

questions.q: R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. What is A⁺?
w: A → B → C → D; E is never reached.

questions.q: Consider R = {A, B, C, D, E, F, G} with FDs {AB → C, B → EF, AD → G}. What is the key for R?
w: AD⁺ = ADG — missing B, C, E, F.
questions.h: A, B, D never appear on the RHS → they must be in the key.

questions.q: R(A, B, C, D, E, F) with F = {A → BC, B → CF, E → A, F → E} (H in an FD is outside R and ignored). How many candidate keys?
w: D is never on the RHS. AD, BD, ED and FD each have closure = all attributes.
questions.h: Never-on-RHS attribute (D) is in every key; A, B, E, F are mutually reachable.

questions.q: For the same relation R(A,B,C,D,E,F) with F = {A → BC, B → CF, E → A, F → E}, the relation is in:
w: C is non-prime and depends on A, which is only PART of the key AD → partial dependency.
questions.h: Non-prime depends on part of a key → violates 2NF.

questions.q: The non-prime attributes of the relation R(A,B,C,D,E) with functional dependencies {AE->BC, AC->D, CD->BE, D->E} is/are:
w: Candidate keys AE, AC, AD use A, C, D, E; only B is in no key.
D and E are also prime.

questions.q: Consider the table R with attributes A, B and C, with FDs A → B, C → AB. Which are true? I. Decomposing R into R1(C, A) and R2(A, B) is lossless. II. Decomposing R into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C) is lossy.
w: I: common A → B, so A is a key of R2 (lossless). II: common B determines nothing (lossy).
questions.h: Lossless if the common attributes are a key of one side.

questions.q: R(A, B, C) with A → B is decomposed into R1(A, B) and R2(A, C). The decomposition is:
w: R1 ∩ R2 = A, and A → B makes A a key of R1.
A → B is kept in R1.
questions.h: Common attribute = key of one part → lossless.

questions.q: Which Armstrong axiom states: if X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z?
w: X → Y, X → Z ⇒ X → YZ.

questions.q: If a relational schema "R" is in BCNF, which of the following statements is true?
o: R is in 2NF but not in 3NF

questions.q: The highest normal form of a relation R(A,B,C,D) with functional dependencies {A->BCD, BC->AD, D->B} is
w: Keys A, BC, CD → all attributes are prime; D → B violates BCNF (D isn't a super key) but B is prime, so 3NF holds.
D → B has a non-super-key LHS.
questions.h: Violation with prime RHS → 3NF but not BCNF.

questions.q: Select the 'False' statement from the following statements about Normal Forms:
o: Lossless preserving decomposition into 3NF is always possible
Any Relation with two attributes is in BCNF
Lossless preserving decomposition into BCNF is always possible
w: False — lossless + dependency-preserving BCNF isn't always possible.
questions.h: 3NF: lossless + preserving ✓. BCNF: lossless ✓, preserving ✗ (not always).

questions.q: A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and:
o: No non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key
Every determinant is a candidate key

questions.q: A relation is in 3NF if for every FD X → A:
o: X is a candidate key only
X is a super key OR A is a prime attribute
questions.h: 3NF: super key LHS or prime RHS.

questions.q: R(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, Grade) with key (StudentID, CourseID) and StudentID → StudentName. The highest normal form is:
w: StudentName depends on part of the key → partial dependency → not 2NF.
questions.h: Part of the key → non-prime = not 2NF.

questions.q: R(EmpID, DeptID, DeptName) with EmpID → DeptID and DeptID → DeptName (key EmpID). The highest normal form is:
w: EmpID → DeptID → DeptName is transitive → not 3NF.

questions.q: Which normal form ensures that every determinant is a candidate key?
w: Every determinant must be a super key.

questions.q: Normalization mainly aims to reduce:
A table where one cell holds several phone numbers ("98xx, 97xx") violates:
Which of the following are true about indexes?
o: Indexes will improve the performance of the database table, even it is updated frequently
Indexes makes sql server engine’s task even tougher, especially with large keys
w: Frequent updates make index maintenance costly.
Large keys mean bigger index trees and more maintenance.

questions.q: A file is structured in such a way that the ordering of data records in certain indexes is the same as or similar to the ordering of data entries. That index is then called
w: Data is physically ordered like the index.

questions.q: An index with an entry for EVERY search-key value is:
Primary indexes of multilevel indexes are created usually based on its first level and it is normally referred as
w: That's an index on the second level.
The index built on the first-level index is the second level.
questions.h: Index on the index = second level.

questions.q: The physical position of a record is calculated by a formula that translates a file key into a position for the record. This is
w: A hash function computes the address.

questions.q: Which index type is best for range queries like salary BETWEEN 10000 AND 20000?
w: Sorted, linked leaves give efficient range scans.

questions.q: A hash index is most suitable for:
Which of the following is/are correct?
o: B-trees are for storing data on disk and B+ trees are for main memory.
Range queries are faster on B+ trees.
B-trees are for primary indexes and B+ trees are for secondary indexes.
The height of a B+ tree is independent of the number of records.
w: Leaves are linked in key order.
questions.h: B+ tree leaves linked → range queries.

questions.q: Which of the following statement(s) is/are not TRUE about the B+ tree, which is used for creating an index of a database table?
o: B+ Tree is a height-balanced tree
Non-leaf nodes have pointers to data records
Key values in each node are kept in sorted order
Each leaf node has a pointer to the next leaf node
w: False — only leaf nodes point to data records.
questions.h: B+ tree: data pointers ONLY in leaves.

questions.q: B+ Trees are normally considered as BALANCED, since
o: Lengths of the paths from the root to all leaf nodes are all equal.
Lengths of the paths from the root to all leaf nodes differ from each other by at most 1
Number of children of any two non-leaf sibling nodes differ by at most 1.
Number of records in any two leaf nodes differ by at most 1
w: All leaves are at the same depth.
questions.h: B+ tree: every leaf at the same level.

questions.q: Find the maximum and minimum number of keys in the internal nodes of a B-Tree if the order of the node is four.
questions.h: Order m: keys between ⌈m/2⌉−1 and m−1.

questions.q: In a B-tree of order 5, the maximum and minimum number of keys in a non-root node are:
Consider a B+-tree in which the maximum number of keys in a node is 7. What is the minimum number of keys in any non-root node?
w: That's the minimum number of children.

questions.q: Consider a B+ tree where the block and node size is 4 kilobytes and each index entry is 40 bytes long. What is the height of the tree for a file with one million search key values?
w: Fan-out n ≈ 100; worst case ⌈log₅₀(1,000,000)⌉ = 4 (nodes at least half full).
That would assume completely full nodes (log₁₀₀).

questions.q: A B-tree of order 4 is constructed by 8 successive insertions from scratch. What is the maximum number of operations for node splitting that can take place?
w: Splits can happen at the 4th, 6th and 8th insertions; the root doesn't overflow within 8 keys.
questions.h: Order 4: a node splits on its 4th key; after the first split, each leaf needs 2 more keys to split again.

questions.q: Consider the query SELECT E.eno, COUNT(*) FROM Employees E GROUP BY E.eno. If an index on eno is available, the query can be answered by scanning only the index if
o: index can be hash or B+ tree and clustered or non-clustered
the index is only hash and clustered
the index is only B+tree and clustered
index can be hash or B+ tree and clustered
w: The index alone has every eno value with its entries — any index type works.
questions.h: Index-only scan: any index on eno works.

questions.q: The 'Durability' property among the ACID properties of a transaction requires that the modifications made by a successful transaction to the database survive.
o: Except in case of an Operating System crash
Always, even if there is a failure of any kind
Except in case of a power failure
Except in case of a Disk crash

questions.q: Which ACID property ensures that a transaction is executed completely or not at all?
Which ACID property is the responsibility of the concurrency-control component?
w: Concurrency control makes concurrent runs look serial.
questions.h: Isolation ↔ concurrency control; A & D ↔ recovery.

questions.q: Which of the following is false? (A) Ensuring durability is the responsibility of the recovery management component (B) Ensuring isolation is the responsibility of concurrency management (C) Ensuring atomicity or consistency is the responsibility of the recovery management component
w: The bank treats it as true.
The bank key: all three statements are considered true.
questions.f: Strictly, consistency is the application programmer's job (Korth), which would make C debatable. The bank key is "None of the options".

questions.q: Which of the following is not a goal of concurrent execution of a transaction?
w: Concurrency INTRODUCES the possibility of deadlocks.
questions.h: Concurrency: + utilisation, + throughput, − waiting; but deadlocks become possible.

questions.q: Which one of the following is true about the concurrency?
o: It ensures that no interference between simultaneous operations on the database
It ensures that a transaction allows either all of its operations are executed or none
It make sure that database transactions allows any integrity violation in the database.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a valid schedule of 2 transactions, T1: {R(X), W(X)} and T2: {R(Y), W(Y)}?
w: Writes come before reads — the order inside each transaction is broken.
questions.h: A schedule must keep each transaction's own order.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs of operations conflict in the transactions T1: {R1(X), W1(X)} and T2: {R2(X), W2(Y)}?
w: Different transactions, same item, one is a write.
questions.h: Conflict = different Tx + same item + ≥ 1 write.

questions.q: Which of the following is a conflict serializable schedule of T1: {R1(X), W1(X), R1(Y)} and T2: {R2(Y), R2(X), W2(X)}?
w: R2(X) before W1(X): T2→T1; R1(X) before W2(X): T1→T2 → cycle.
All conflicts point T1 → T2 → acyclic.
questions.h: Draw the precedence graph; no cycle = conflict serializable.

questions.q: The schedule S: r1(X), w3(X), w3(Y), w2(Y), r1(Z), w3(Z), w2(Z) is
o: Both view serializable and conflict serializable schedule
View serializable but not conflict serializable schedule
w: Edges T1→T3, T3→T2, T1→T2 → acyclic (order T1, T3, T2).

questions.q: For the given schedule S : r1(y), r2(x), r2(y), r3(y), w2(x), w1(y), w3(x), r1(x), which is true?
o: S is the conflict serializable but not view serializable
S is neither conflict serializable nor view serializable
S is both conflict serializable as well as view serializable
S is view serializable but not conflict serializable
w: Edges T2→T1, T3→T1, T2→T3 → order T2, T3, T1.

questions.q: Schedule: R1(A), R2(A), W1(A), W2(A). Is it conflict serializable?
o: No — the precedence graph has a cycle T1 ⇄ T2
w: R2(A) before W1(A) gives T2 → T1.
R1(A) before W2(A) gives T1 → T2.

questions.q: Which of the following statement is not correct for serializable of transactions?
o: In a serial schedule, each transaction is independent of others.
In non-serial schedule may not always result in an incorrect outcome
In non-serial schedule, may result with overlapping of two transaction’s executions

questions.q: Consider S : r1(x), w1(x), r2(x), r1(y), w1(y), w2(x), r2(y), c1, c2. I: S is recoverable. II: If the order of w1(x) and w2(x) is interchanged, S will be non-recoverable. Which is true?
w: T2 reads from T1 and T1 commits first → recoverable. Swapping the writes keeps T1 committing first, so it stays recoverable → II is false.
questions.h: Recoverable: the writer commits before the reader commits.

questions.q: Which one of the following events in a database system can lead to an irrecoverable mistake?
o: A transaction reads a data item after it is written by an uncommitted transaction
A transaction reads a data item after it is written by a committed transaction
A transaction reads a data item after it is read by an uncommitted transaction
A transaction writes a data item after it is read by an uncommitted transaction
w: Dirty read: if the reader commits and the writer aborts, it can't be undone.

questions.q: A cascading rollback happens when:
o: The failure of one transaction forces others that read its uncommitted data to roll back

questions.q: Which of the following will not allow both dirty reads and non-repeatable reads, but allows phantom reads?
w: Prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads; phantoms may still appear.
questions.h: RU → RC (no dirty) → RR (no non-repeatable) → S (no phantoms).

questions.q: The isolation level that prevents dirty reads but still allows non-repeatable reads is:
w: Reads only committed data, but a value can change between two reads.
questions.h: Read committed = no dirty reads only.

questions.q: Which isolation level allows dirty reads?
Which level of locking provides the highest degree of concurrency in a relational database?
o: Page, table and row level locking allow the same degree of concurrency
w: The finest granularity → most transactions can run in parallel.

questions.q: The two-phase locking protocol guarantees:
w: The lock point gives a serial order.

questions.q: In two-phase locking, the growing phase is when a transaction:
o: May obtain locks but not release any
May release locks but not obtain any
w: Then the shrinking phase releases locks only.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE? I. Strict two-phase locking produces conflict serializable schedules which are not recoverable. II. Timestamp ordering with Thomas’ Write Rule can produce view serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable.
w: I is false: strict 2PL schedules are recoverable (strict).
Thomas' write rule ignores obsolete blind writes → view but not conflict serializable.

questions.q: Which of the following is true?
o: All the schedules which are allowed under Thomas write rule are also allowed under basic timestamp protocol
All the schedules which are allowed under basic timestamp rule are also allowed under multi-version timestamp protocol
All the schedules which are allowed under multi-version timestamp protocol are also allowed under Thomas write rule
w: MVTO is more permissive than basic TO.
questions.h: Basic TO ⊆ MVTO; Basic TO ⊆ Thomas.

questions.q: Which of the following is correct with respect to Two phase commit protocol?
w: The bank's answer (it treats the two-phase protocol as guaranteeing correct, serializable outcomes).
questions.f: Strictly, 2-phase COMMIT ensures atomic commit across distributed sites; 2-phase LOCKING is what ensures serializability. Pick the bank key here, because none of the deadlock options apply.

questions.q: Two-phase commit (2PC) is primarily used for:
o: Ensuring atomic commit of a distributed transaction across multiple sites
questions.h: 2PC = all sites commit or all abort.

questions.q: In the wait-die deadlock prevention scheme, if an older transaction requests a lock held by a younger one:
o: The older transaction is rolled back
The younger transaction is killed immediately
w: That happens to the younger one in the reverse case.
questions.h: Wait-die: old waits, young dies. Wound-wait: old wounds young.

questions.q: Optimistic (validation-based) concurrency control is best when:
w: Transactions run freely and are validated at commit.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a recovery technique?
w: A distributed commit protocol, not a recovery method.
The bank treats it as recovery.

questions.q: Rollback of transactions is normally used to :
In the deferred update recovery technique, after a crash the system needs:
w: Uncommitted changes never reached the database.

questions.q: In the immediate update technique, recovery may need:
w: Uncommitted changes may be on disk.
Committed changes may not be on disk yet.

questions.q: The write-ahead logging (WAL) rule says:
o: The log record must be written to stable storage before the corresponding data page is written
Data pages are written before the log
The log is written only at shutdown
w: So changes can always be undone or redone.

questions.q: The purpose of a checkpoint in log-based recovery is to:
o: Reduce the amount of log that must be scanned after a crash
w: Everything before the checkpoint is already safe on disk.

questions.q: Which recovery technique maintains two page tables and does not need undo logs?
w: The current table is updated; the shadow table is kept unchanged until commit.

questions.q: Which of the following are the NoSQL databases?
w: One type, but not the only one.
Key-value, wide-column and document stores are all NoSQL types (and graph databases).
questions.h: NoSQL family: key-value, document, wide-column, graph.
questions.f: Correction: the bank key says "Key-value", but all three listed types are NoSQL databases. In the real exam, the key may say "Key-value".

questions.q: NoSQL databases is used mainly for handling large volumes of ______________ data.
w: The bank's answer: NoSQL suits unstructured data that doesn't fit tables.
Also handled, but the bank key is unstructured.

questions.q: Which of the following statement(s) are incorrect
o: In non-relational databases, schemas are need to be defined before adding data
NoSQL databases allows the insertion of data without a predefined schema
NewSQL databases allows the insertion of data without a predefined schema
w: The bank treats this as correct.

questions.q: MongoDB is an example of which type of NoSQL database?
Cassandra and HBase are examples of:
Neo4j is best suited for:
o: Graph data such as social networks and relationships

questions.q: The CAP theorem states a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee:
w: At most two of the three.
